stories.title: Northmarq Closes Sale of $23M Multifamily Community in Spokane
stories.excerpt: Northmarq’s Seattle Investment Sales team, led by Tyler Smith, Steve Fischer, Joe Kinkopf and Brendan Greenheck, brokered the $22.5 million sale of Go Go Heights Apartments, a 178-unit garden-style multifamily community located at 7024 N. Colton St. in Spokane, Washington. Northmarq represented the seller, LC Gogo Heights LLC, in the transaction. The buyer was c702 LLC, a Washington-based private investment firm. ”There were a lot of market headwinds in getting this transaction to the finish line,” Kinkopf said. “The buyer was able to leverage their local team in order to execute on this deal quickly and successfully.” The transaction reflects continued investor interest in well-located multifamily assets throughout the Pacific Northwest, particularly properties that offer scale and long-term value in growing regional markets. Constructed in 1989, Go Go Heights Apartments offer residents a mix of two- and three-bedroom units featuring hardwood laminate flooring, walk-in closets, in-unit fireplaces, vaulted ceilings and private balconies. If you’re reading about the multifamily industry, you should be in the room with its leaders. Connect Apartments brings together the executives featured in Connect CRE’s coverage for an afternoon of high-level insights and unmatched networking on September 22 at The Biltmore in LA. The post Northmarq Closes Sale of $23M Multifamily Community in Spokane appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Northmarq brokered $22.5M sale of 178-unit Go Go Heights Apartments in Spokane, WA.
Buyer c702 LLC, local Washington firm; seller LC Gogo Heights LLC; 1989 garden-style property.
Broker cited market headwinds but closed deal; signals continued PNW multifamily investor appetite.
stories.summary: Northmarq's Seattle team sold Go Go Heights Apartments, a 178-unit garden-style community in Spokane, for $22.5 million to c702 LLC. The 1989-built property offers two- and three-bedroom units. Despite market headwinds, the transaction closed, reflecting persistent investor interest in well-located, scaled multifamily assets in growing Pacific Northwest regional markets.
stories.impact: Deal closure signals that despite financing friction, institutional and local investors remain active acquirers of stabilized, secondary-market multifamily. Spokane's appeal as a value-add acquisition market remains intact; implies demand for below-replacement-cost assets in mid-tier Western metros persists into 2026.

stories.title: JBL Asset Management Buys Retail Condo Near Miami Design District
stories.excerpt: Alta Developers sold off a retail condo near the Miami Design District for $17.3 million, property records show. JBL Asset Management purchased the 25,504-square-foot asset on the ground floor of the Quadro condo building. The property at 3900 Biscayne Boulevard faces train tracks, just east of the Miami Design District, an open-air, luxury mall. Quadro’s retail tenants include The Shade Store, 7th Avenue furniture store and Waterworks plumbing supply store. Hollywood, Fla.-based JBL is marketing a 2,358-square-foot suite as the last remaining retail space at the 407,498-square-foot condo building. Alta Developers completed the 200-unit building in 2019. The purchase comes as the 18-block Design District, one of the country’s highest-grossing upscale malls, is undergoing a major expansion. Earlier this week, its owners, entities tied to Miami-based Craig Robins and LVMH billionaire Bernard Arnault, scored a $125 million construction loan to build a Snøhetta-designed, mixed-use building. The joint venture also launched sales for Fouquet’s condo and hotel development, designed by Pritzker Prize winner David Chipperfield. Representatives for Alta Developers and JBL Asset Management did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Julia Echikson can be reached at jechikson@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: JBL Asset Management acquired 25,504-sf retail condo ground floor, 3900 Biscayne Boulevard, Miami for $17.3M.
Alta Developers sold property; Design District undergoing major expansion with $125M construction loan approved.
Quadro building retail tenants include The Shade Store, furniture, plumbing; last 2,358-sf suite being marketed.
stories.summary: Alta Developers sold a 25,504-square-foot retail condo on the ground floor of the Quadro building near Miami's Design District to JBL Asset Management for $17.3 million. The property faces train tracks on Biscayne Boulevard. The Design District, a luxury open-air mall, is undergoing major expansion, with ownership securing a $125 million construction loan for new mixed-use development.
stories.impact: Design District expansion (hotel/condo tower, Fouquet's by Chipperfield, $125M loan close) signals accelerating foot traffic and real estate investment velocity in the submarket. Multifamily developers should monitor Edgewater/Biscayne corridor and nearby residential submarkets for emerging demand from affluent Design District workers, residents, and visitors; proximity to luxury retail/dining/hospitality supports premium rents.

stories.title: Williamson County Greenlights $674M Blue Origin Development Deal
stories.excerpt: Two weeks ago, Connect reported that the Williamson County economic development board had agreed to terms with Jeff Bezos’ space technology company, Blue Origin. Yesterday, the full board of commissioners approved the item, and it raises the odds that the company will build a $674 million facility in Hutto, within Williamson County. There is still one more approval required. The State of Texas needs to okay the deal. The approval would facilitate Blue Origin’s construction of approximately one million square-feet of industrial research space related to the aerospace and defense industry, located in Hutto Crossing industrial park. The facility would create as many as 2,000 jobs in 10 years. That 10-year deal includes a county abatement of 100% of real property and 50% of personal property taxes in the first five years, and 50% on real property in the last five years.  Founded in 2000, Blue Origin aims to develop reusable rocket technology to lower the cost of space travel and make it more accessible. The post Williamson County Greenlights $674M Blue Origin Development Deal appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Williamson County commissioners approved $674M Blue Origin aerospace/defense facility in Hutto, Texas.
Project: ~1M sf industrial R&D; 2,000 jobs over 10 years; 100% property tax abatement 5 years, 50% remaining 5.
State of Texas must approve final; Hutto Crossing industrial park location; deal enables major employer anchor.
stories.summary: Williamson County approved a $674 million Blue Origin facility in Hutto, Texas comprising approximately one million square feet of aerospace and defense research space. The project is expected to create as many as 2,000 jobs over ten years. The deal includes 100% real property tax abatement for five years and 50% for the final five, pending state-level approval.
stories.impact: Blue Origin's 2,000-job, decade-long ramp in Hutto is a major employer anchor that will drive population in-migration and household formation in the Austin metro's northern corridor. Multifamily developers should acquire/entitle residential across Williamson County (Hutto, Pflugerville, Round Rock submarket) ahead of job and wage growth; the aerospace/defense sector attracts higher-income workers, supporting class A/B product. Tax abatement signals pro-growth incentives; timing window to break ground before supply tightens.

stories.title: Now Is the Time to Buy in Commercial Real Estate: Morgan Stanley
stories.excerpt: Despite a bumpy economy and increasingly high Treasury yields, one global investment firm believes now is the time to pounce on U.S. commercial real estate. Commercial Observer spoke with Tony Charles, global head of research and strategy at Morgan Stanley Real Estate Investing, who outlined the main takeaways from Morgan Stanley Investment Management’s mid-year 2026 real estate outlook. After a four-year recession, commercial real estate is now being repriced, giving investors a chance to acquire prime assets at low prices; supply is down across the board; and megatrends in AI, global supply chains, and aging demographics have opened up attractive entry points into infrastructure, retail and senior housing. “We certainly believe we’re entering the next up-cycle for real estate. It’s an attractive entry point,” Charles told CO in a Thursday interview. “And, given the repricing that’s now below replacement costs, we’re pretty confident in the next vintage of real estate investing.” Charles argued that the recent U.S. real estate downturn — which began in mid-2022 amid the Federal Reserve’s policy U-turn to hike interest rates coming out of COVID-19 — created “the longest downturn for real estate since the 1980s and early 1990s,” and that four years later, pricing is still down an average of 20 percent across the board. But he noted that “supply is down dramatically, so that’s obviously very helpful for real estate,” and that a strong structural macroeconomic backdrop — U.S. GDP grew 2.1 percent year-over-year in the second quarter of 2026 — has provided “a lot of green shoots that are beginning to show through.” He pointed out that CRE transaction activity increased 23 percent year-over-year in the U.S., institutional capital raising is up nearly 40 percent on the year, and that CRE debt originations are up around 20 percent year-over-year. bullets: Morgan Stanley REIM: U.S. CRE repricing below replacement cost; entering next up-cycle; supply down board.
Megatrends (AI, supply chains, aging demographics) opening attractive entry points in infrastructure, retail, senior housing.
Four-year CRE recession ending; improved capital conditions and cap rate stability signal investor confidence return.
stories.summary: Morgan Stanley Real Estate Investing's mid-year 2026 outlook argues the U.S. is entering the next real estate up-cycle, with assets repricing below replacement cost and supply constraints across property types. Megatrends in AI, global supply chains, and aging demographics are creating attractive entry points. The firm expects renewed institutional capital deployment through the remainder of 2026.
stories.impact: Morgan Stanley's bullish stance on next-cycle entry points signals institutional capital appetite is returning to CRE. For multifamily developers: cap rates and financing conditions are stabilizing, replacement-cost underwriting supports new development feasibility. Focus on high-growth metros (Sunbelt, tech hubs) and demographic tailwinds (aging, younger renter cohorts) to attract capital; thesis validates value-creation through new supply in supply-constrained markets.

stories.title: Lincoln, ACORE Converting Historic SLC Foundry
stories.excerpt: Lincoln Property Company and ACORE CAPITAL launched Foundry43, the new identity for the former Industry SLC historic structure. The property was created through the adaptive reuse of a distinctive industrial landmark in Salt Lake City. (photo courtesy Salt Lake Tribune) ACORE enlisted Lincoln to help stabilize and reposition this mixed-use development at the former steel foundry site. Together, the partners have been making meaningful investments into the property to restart construction and have now completed the parking structure and retail space. The Former Industry SLC building Reimagined as Foundry43 will build upon the existing 230,000 square foot office campus by delivering 64,000 square feet of additional creative office space, a 34,000 square foot fitness center, 12,000 square feet of new retail, and a 1,000-stall parking garage in the heart of the Granary Neighborhood. JLL has been retained to lead leasing efforts for the property. The post Lincoln, ACORE Converting Historic SLC Foundry appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Lincoln Property Company and ACORE Capital repositioning historic Industry SLC foundry as Foundry43 mixed-use.
Completed parking structure (1,000 stalls), retail (12,000 sf); delivering 64,000 sf office, 34,000 sf fitness, 12,000 sf retail.
230,000 sf existing office campus expanded; JLL retained for leasing; Granary Neighborhood location, Salt Lake City.
stories.summary: Lincoln Property Company and ACORE Capital launched Foundry43, an adaptive reuse of a historic steel foundry in Salt Lake City's Granary Neighborhood. The partners have restarted construction, completing parking and retail infrastructure. The project will deliver 64,000 square feet of creative office space, a 34,000-square-foot fitness center, 12,000 square feet of retail, and a 1,000-stall garage alongside the existing 230,000-square-foot office campus.
stories.impact: Adaptive reuse mixed-use repositioning in Salt Lake's Granary (walkable, trendy urban neighborhood) signals strong demand for live-work-play urban infill, particularly among younger professionals. Neighboring multifamily developers should note strong co-tenancy drivers (office, fitness, retail, parking); proximity to Foundry43 supports market-rate and premium apartment development; SLC's tech/finance growth and amenity clustering make adjacent residential sites highly desirable.

stories.title: RangeWater Spends $55M on Atlanta Rental Community
stories.excerpt: Bell Partners sold Bell Buckhead West for $54.9 million. RangeWater Residential was the buyer. Bell Partners paid $62 million to acquire the asset in 2017, which is at 3201 Downwood Cir. in Atlanta. RangeWater renamed the property Blaine Buckhead West. Rents at Blaine Buckhead West range from $1,399 to $2,345. Unit sizes range from 676 square feet for a studio to 1,189 square feet for a two-bedroom unit. The 280-unit project was built in 2015. Amenities include a fitness center, pool, 24-hour Java Bar and Lounge, Bocce Ball Court, game room with pool table, and a Sky Lounge Rooftop Deck. Sun Life Financial announced acquired Bell Partners for $350 million. As part of the arrangement, Bell Partners became part of Sun Life’s multifamily operating platform. The post RangeWater Spends $55M on Atlanta Rental Community appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: RangeWater acquired Bell Buckhead West (280 units) from Bell Partners for $54.9M; renamed Blaine Buckhead West.
Bell Partners paid $62M in 2017; built 2015; rents $1,399–$2,345; unit mix studio (676 sf) to 2-bed (1,189 sf).
Sun Life Financial acquired Bell Partners for $350M; Bell Partners now part of Sun Life's multifamily operating platform.
stories.summary: RangeWater Residential purchased Bell Buckhead West, a 280-unit garden-style community in Atlanta, for $54.9 million. Bell Partners, the prior owner, had acquired the asset in 2017 for $62 million. Rents range from $1,399 to $2,345. Bell Partners is now part of Sun Life Financial's multifamily operating platform after a $350 million acquisition.
stories.impact: Sale at $54.9M (vs. $62M 2017 acquisition price) reflects valuation compression but RangeWater's entry signals confidence in Atlanta's rental market fundamentals and operator upside. Sun Life's $350M Bell Partners acquisition and platform build-out indicate institutional insurance-linked capital is deploying into multifamily operations; expect Sun Life to be an active acquirer and developer in Sunbelt markets. Buckhead West submarket remains sought-after; recovery from pandemic-era pricing lows underway.

stories.title: Whole Foods to Open Daily Shop at Murray Hill’s 509 Third Avenue
stories.excerpt: Whole Foods Market has leased a 9,000-square-foot retail space in Manhattan’s Murray Hill neighborhood. The 15-year deal occupies a ground-floor space and outdoor terraces at 509 Third Avenue, according to a memorandum of lease filed in city records Friday morning. The 35-story, 229-unit apartment tower, known as the Murray, was developed by Kahen Properties with Lalezarian Properties. A spokesperson for Whole Foods confirmed the lease in an email to Commercial Observer, but declined to share further details. Whole Foods’ newest Manhattan location will be on the smaller side. The store will follow the Amazon-owned grocer’s new Whole Foods Market Daily Shop format. The quick-trip urban shops sell grab-and-go meals alongside fresh produce, meat, bakery items and local specialty foods, according to the company’s website. The format was first rolled out in nearby Lenox Hill in 2024, and has since arrived in cities nationwide. Additional locations in Brooklyn and Hoboken, N.J., were announced late last year. Most recently, the grocer signed a lease for 8,121 square feet to open a daily shop at 1524 Second Avenue on the Upper East Side. Kahen Properties’ Majid Kahen signed the lease memorandum for the landlord, while Paul Hilliard, vice president of real estate at Whole Foods, signed for the grocer. It is unclear whether either party worked with an outside brokerage. The asking rent for the ground-floor space was not disclosed in the memorandum, but retail space in the nearby Herald Square area was $394 per square foot during the second quarter of 2026, according to CBRE data. Spokespeople for Kahen and Lalezarian Properties did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Emily Davis can be reached at edavis@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Whole Foods Market leased 9,000 sf ground floor + terraces at 509 Third Avenue, Murray Hill, Manhattan (15-year deal).
Store format: Whole Foods Market Daily Shop (grab-and-go, fresh produce, meat, bakery, local specialty foods).
Murray building: 35-story, 229-unit apartment tower by Kahen Properties and Lalezarian Properties; first Daily Shop in Lenox Hill rolled out 2024.
stories.summary: Whole Foods Market leased a 9,000-square-foot ground-floor retail space with outdoor terraces at 509 Third Avenue in Manhattan's Murray Hill neighborhood for 15 years. The store will operate as a Whole Foods Market Daily Shop, a smaller format offering grab-and-go meals and fresh grocery items. The space is located in the Murray, a 35-story, 229-unit apartment tower developed by Kahen and Lalezarian Properties.
stories.impact: Whole Foods Daily Shop anchor in Murray Hill (Upper East Side's younger, less-expensive submarket) signals Amazon's retail expansion into accessible price points and urban convenience formats. For multifamily: quality ground-floor food retail (especially premium grocery) is a strong co-tenancy driver for rents and lease-up velocity in Manhattan rental buildings. Murray's 229-unit apartment tower benefits directly from foot traffic and retail amenity; developers in emerging Manhattan submarkets should prioritize grocery/food tenants to enhance unit positioning and achievable rents.

stories.title: Medical Outpatient Building Sales Surge in H1 2026
stories.excerpt: Improving capital market conditions, expanding lender appetite and resilient operating fundamentals have driven a surge in medical outpatient building (MOB) investment sales activity, Cushman & Wakefield reported. MOB transaction volume reached $6.7 billion in the first half of 2026, a 21% increase year-over-year. MOB cap rates, meanwhile, declined 35 basis points Y-O-Y to 6.8%, while average asset pricing reached $368 per square foot in Q2 2026. Portfolio transaction activity more than doubled relative to H1 2025, exceeding $2.6 billion, as the portfolio premium widened to 100 bps over single-asset cap rates. “Cap rate compression, renewed debt market liquidity, and rising portfolio demand all point to improving investor confidence, while steady rent growth and high occupancy levels reinforce the sector’s underlying fundamentals,” said Sandy Romero, head of office & alternatives research at Cushman & Wakefield. “With capital becoming more readily available, we expect MOBs to remain well-positioned to attract institutional investment through the balance of 2026.” The post Medical Outpatient Building Sales Surge in H1 2026 appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: MOB transaction volume: $6.7B in H1 2026, +21% YoY; cap rates compressed 35 bps to 6.8%; average pricing $368/sf Q2 2026.
Portfolio transaction activity more than doubled vs. H1 2025, exceeding $2.6B; portfolio premium widened to 100 bps.
Cushman & Wakefield: capital availability, rent growth, high occupancy reinforce MOB fundamentals; expects sustained institutional investment through 2026.
stories.summary: Medical outpatient building (MOB) investment sales surged to $6.7 billion in H1 2026, a 21% year-over-year increase, driven by improving capital markets, lender appetite, and strong operating fundamentals. MOB cap rates declined 35 basis points to 6.8%, while average pricing reached $368 per square foot in Q2. Portfolio transaction activity more than doubled, exceeding $2.6 billion, with portfolio premiums widening to 100 basis points over single-asset cap rates.
stories.impact: MOB strength (cap rate compression, portfolio demand, +$2.6B portfolio activity) reflects institutional capital rotation into healthcare real estate amid demographic aging and outpatient care shift. For multifamily developers: healthtech/medical office co-tenancy in mixed-use or nearby residential projects enhances NOI and marketing (affluent patient/staff base). MOB capital strength also indicates available institutional debt capital; multifamily developers should expect competitive financing conditions and potential cross-collateralization opportunities in healthcare-anchored markets.

stories.title: Shifting Fortunes for L.A.’s Ports Boost Surrounding Industrial Real Estate
stories.excerpt: Ports are meant to offer protection from storms or rough seas. But nothing has been able to protect the ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach from the uncertainty and fluctuation of trade policy during President Donald Trump’s second term. “It’s like the quote from ‘The Morning Show,’” said Gregg Healy, executive vice president and head of Savills Industrial Services. “Chaos is the new cocaine. I do think we will have more turbulent times ahead.” So it’s been a welcome surprise that the tariff turbulence has seemed to benefit industrial real estate near or tied to the waterfront. From Liberation Day in April 2025, when Trump announced his first round of sweeping tariffs, to the current war with Iran, the ebbs and flows of global trade have been massive and disruptive, but new shipping volume is helping port-adjacent and port-dependent submarkets. Amid a boom and bust cycle that’s dominated the last few years, and pushing warehouse vacancy to a recent peak of 7 percent this year, Los Angeles’ industrial side may be poised for an upswing. People watch as a container ship departs from the Port of Los Angeles. PHOTO: Mario Tama/Getty Images Shipping volume at the ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach is up 1.8 percent this year. After topping 1 million container units in June, the Port of Los Angeles nearly hit that mark in July, making it the second-busiest July on record. “Businesses continue to move cargo when they see windows of opportunity amid an evolving trade environment, while resilient consumer demand is helping keep imports at historically strong levels,” said Port of Los Angeles Executive Director Gene Seroka in a recent statement. The region’s industrial market saw its highest leasing levels in five years during the second quarter of 2026, according to Cushman & Wakefield data, driven by its centrality to larger logistics networks. bullets: L.A./Long Beach port volumes volatile amid Trump tariff cycles (April 2025 Liberation Day through Iran conflict).
Port-adjacent and port-dependent industrial submarkets benefiting from tariff flux, shipping volume surges.
Los Angeles warehouse vacancy peaked at ~7% this year; industrial side poised for upswing amid boom-bust cycle.
stories.summary: Trade policy uncertainty under President Trump's second term has created volatility at the Ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach, but port-adjacent and port-dependent industrial real estate has benefited from shifting shipping volumes. Despite a recent warehouse vacancy peak near 7%, new shipping activity is driving demand in port-tied submarkets. Analysts expect continued turbulence but near-term upside for industrial real estate near the waterfront.
stories.impact: Tariff volatility is creating short-term shipping volume swings that benefit port-adjacent industrial; however, sustained policy uncertainty may dampen long-term logistics real estate investment. Multifamily developers should avoid over-relying on port-adjacent job growth; instead, monitor broad Southland employment trends. If tariff cycles stabilize in favor of U.S. nearshoring/reshoring, logistics hub strength (inland Empire, Long Beach submarket) could drive wage/job growth supporting regional multifamily demand. Track tariff policy shifts as a market timing signal.

stories.title: Retail Landlords Need to Underwrite Their Tenants’ Customer Base, Too
stories.excerpt: Landlords underwrite the retail tenant. But they almost never underwrite the tenant’s customer. They should. That gap costs landlords money, and it is fixable before a listing goes live. The standard leasing process is too reactive: Review comparable rents, post the space on Crexi and LoopNet, wait for responses, and then vet an operator’s finances. Mark Kvetkovskiy. None of that tells you whether enough of that retailer’s customers live near the space. If they do not, the risk rises of tenant failure, months of vacancy, and another round of commissions and negotiations. The better approach is to flip the process. Instead of waiting to see who shows up, start by studying who lives near the space. How do nearby households spend? Which categories over-index locally? Does the neighborhood support an everyday concept, a destination brand, or something in between? Answer those questions first, and you can define the customer already walking the neighborhood’s streets. Then, identify the brands that serve that customer and approach them directly about the vacancy. Proactive outreach can reduce days on market and the vacancy costs that come with them. Consider a hypothetical vacant restaurant at Rivington and Ludlow streets on Manhattan’s Lower East Side. I analyzed the 2026 Esri Consumer Spending Survey and Esri Market Potential data for the area within a five-minute walk. Esri’s modeled data draws on consumer surveys, demographic segmentation and household spending patterns. It is directional, not a record of observed transactions. Esri estimates that households in that walking area spend $50,243,250 annually on food and beverages away from home, or about $5,043 per household. The market-potential data then sharpens the picture. Some 20.4 percent of adults in the area visited a fine-dining restaurant in the previous six months, an index of 124, or 24 percent above the U.S. average. bullets: Retail landlords underwrite tenant finances but rarely underwrite tenant's customer base and local household spending.
Gap creates tenant failure risk, vacancy, and commission costs; proactive customer profiling before listing reduces days-on-market.
Better approach: study nearby household demographics, spending patterns, brand alignment before leasing outreach; direct landlord-to-brand negotiation faster than reactive posting.
stories.summary: Retail landlords typically underwrite tenant creditworthiness but fail to validate whether the tenant's customer base lives in proximity to the space. This gap increases risk of tenant failure and extended vacancy. A more proactive approach involves analyzing local household demographics and spending patterns first, then directly recruiting aligned retail brands, rather than posting and waiting for responses.
stories.impact: Insight applies indirectly to multifamily: strong retail tenants (grocery, dining, fitness) drive footfall and renter willingness-to-pay. Multifamily developers should adopt same "customer-first" lens when planning ground-floor retail in new buildings—profile the renter demographic first, then recruit tenants serving that demographic directly. Avoiding misaligned retail (which cannibalizes foot traffic and resident satisfaction) is critical to lease-up and NOI. Co-tenant quality compounds unit rent potential more than unit quality alone.
